abstract: Nuclear read-outs on an organ-on-a-chip (cell number, proliferation, viability) start from a nuclear stain, but fixation ends the experiment, live DNA dyes add phototoxic exposure, and reporter lines are impractical for primary or iPSC-derived tissue. In-silico labeling (ISL) predicts the stain from bright-field, but a point prediction gives no warning when it is wrong. ChipStain predicts the H2B nuclear channel from one bright-field image together with a per-pixel uncertainty σ (U-Net with an ImageNet ResNet-34 encoder, β-NLL heteroscedastic head, 8× test-time augmentation). We validate the uncertainty, not only the image, on a public HeLa time-lapse in a 96-well plate (held-out well, 125 images, 3 training seeds; no chip data were available to us). Against a matched control — the same ImageNet U-Net trained with L1 and the same augmentation — ChipStain has the same correlation with the real stain (r {{n_full_pearson}} vs {{n_pm_pearson}}) at {{n_pm_mae_rel}} % higher pixel error, and its σ ranks pixel errors better (Spearman ρ {{n_full_rho}} vs {{n_pm_rho}}; AUSE {{n_full_ause}} vs {{n_pm_ause}}; in every seed). σ is approximately calibrated without recalibration (nominal 95 % intervals cover {{n_cal_95}} % of pixels). Under simulated blur or a phase-contrast input every model fails and σ is not a reliable drift alarm, but a cheap input check (image focus plus encoder-feature distance) flags all of these images, at {{n_qc_focus_gate_clean}} % false alarms on clean images. Gating frames by σ lowers the mean bias of label-free doubling times from {{n_pl_cs_bias_all}} % to {{n_pl_cs_bias_gate}} %, mostly by routing failing fields to review. For counting alone, a direct bright-field segmenter is more accurate (Cellpose F1 {{n_cp_f1}} vs {{n_full_segf1}}); ChipStain's value is a fluorescence-like image with a calibrated trust signal. Open code and weights; CPU inference.

calibration_text: ChipStain + TTA is close to calibrated without any correction: the nominal 68.3 % and 95 % intervals cover {{n_cal_68}} % and {{n_cal_95_raw1}} % of test pixels; the scale fitted on the validation split would be ×{{n_cal_scale}} (after it, the 95 % interval covers {{n_cal_95_recal}} %). Coverage is pooled over pixels, most of which are background; restricted to pixels inside the reference nuclei, the 95 % interval covers {{n_cal_fg95}} %. The TTA disagreement of the L1 U-Nets is far too small to be read as a standard deviation (the matched ImageNet U-Net's 68.3 % interval covers {{n_cal_pm_68}} %; it needs scaling by ×{{n_cal_pm_scale}}, the scratch U-Net by ×{{n_cal_unet_scale}}): it can rank errors but not quantify them. Calibration holds in distribution only: under imaging shift (§6.7) σ does not track the much larger error in most training runs.
shift_text: All models' predictions degrade under blur and the modality swap (Figure 6A), and ChipStain is not more robust than the L1 models: under blur it lies between them, with phase contrast it is the worst (mean Pearson r under 1 px blur {{n_shift_cs_r_def1}} for ChipStain vs {{n_shift_pre_r_def1}} for the matched ImageNet U-Net and {{n_shift_bu_r_def1}} for the scratch U-Net; with phase contrast {{n_shift_cs_r_dpc}} vs {{n_shift_pre_r_dpc}} and {{n_shift_bu_r_dpc}}). Whether σ then rises is a property of the individual training run rather than of the method (Figure 6B, one dot per seed): mean σ separates blurred from clean images (AUROC > 0.8) in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_ok}} ChipStain seeds, {{n_shift_pre_defocus_seeds_ok}} ImageNet-U-Net seeds and {{n_shift_bu_defocus_seeds_ok}} scratch-U-Net seeds, and falls under blur (AUROC < 0.2, a silent failure) in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_down}}, {{n_shift_pre_defocus_seeds_down}} and {{n_shift_bu_defocus_seeds_down}} seeds respectively. Averaged over seeds, ChipStain's σ is the weakest shift detector of the three (shift-detection AUROC for blur {{n_shift_cs_sig_defocus}} vs {{n_shift_pre_sig_defocus}} and {{n_shift_bu_sig_defocus}}; phase contrast {{n_shift_cs_sig_dpc}} vs {{n_shift_pre_sig_dpc}} and {{n_shift_bu_sig_dpc}}; failure detection {{n_shift_cs_sig_fail}} vs {{n_shift_pre_sig_fail}} and {{n_shift_bu_sig_fail}}; Tables 7a–b). Where a signal appears, it comes from the TTA disagreement, not from the learned β-NLL head: the single-pass learned σ has the lowest shift AUROC of all terms (blur {{n_shift_cs_sig_single_pass_defocus}}, phase contrast {{n_shift_cs_sig_single_pass_dpc}}). The released seed-0 checkpoint is one of the runs whose total σ rises (×{{n_shift_cs_s0_def4x}} under 4 px blur, ×{{n_shift_cs_s0_dpcx}} with phase contrast), which is what the demo shows; with the same checkpoint the single-pass learned σ actually falls on the blurred demo image. Additive noise of 10–20 % raises total σ in every model and seed (shift-detection AUROC ≥ 0.98); the validation-calibrated gate flags 97–100 % of noisy images for ChipStain and the scratch U-Net but only 59–67 % for the ImageNet-L1 U-Net. Affine contrast changes were not tested, because the per-image normalisation cancels them exactly. Conclusion: in distribution ChipStain's σ ranks errors well and is calibrated (§6.5); out of distribution neither its σ nor TTA disagreement is a dependable drift alarm. An input check does this job better (below).
ensemble_text: Combining the three training seeds, a deep ensemble of plain U-Nets yields a poor uncertainty (ρ {{n_ens_bu_rho}}, AUSE {{n_ens_bu_ause}}): with three members, the disagreement of point predictors is too noisy to rank errors. An ensemble of ImageNet-initialised L1 U-Nets does better (ρ {{n_ens_pre_rho}}, AUSE {{n_ens_pre_ause}}) but still trails a single ChipStain model with TTA. A ChipStain ensemble without TTA gives the best ranking among β = 0.5 configurations (ρ {{n_ens_cs_rho}}, AUSE {{n_ens_cs_ause}}; the plain-NLL head with TTA ranks errors better still, ρ {{n_b0tta_rho}}, AUSE {{n_b0tta_ause}}, at a large fidelity cost — §6.3), and with TTA it reaches Pearson r {{n_ens_cstta_pearson}} and seg-F1 {{n_ens_cstta_segf1}}, absorbing single-seed failures. Three models triple the cost, so the single TTA model is the released default.
counting_text: Counting nuclei on the prediction with a fixed, simple watershed reaches F1 {{n_full_segf1}} (ChipStain + TTA) against the StarDist reference; the same watershed on the real stain reaches {{n_real_segf1}}, so much of the gap to perfect agreement is the segmenter (Appendix A). Count agreement is better than object agreement because merges and splits partly cancel. A biologist will ask whether one should predict the stain at all if the goal is a count. The dataset author's Cellpose model, trained on this dataset's training split to segment nuclei directly from bright-field (and quality-controlled by its author on this held-out well), reaches F1 {{n_cp_f1}} on the same test images with a mean count error of {{n_cp_count_err}} % (Table 8) — better than counting on our prediction, and better than our watershed on the real stain, because it was trained to reproduce exactly the StarDist label definition used as reference. For counting alone, direct segmentation is the better tool. {{cellpose_pred_text}}ISL earns its place differently: it returns an intensity image that any downstream pipeline can use (intensity, texture, chromatin condensation, morphology — not only outlines), and a calibrated uncertainty. {{cellpose_shift_text}}We also tested whether ChipStain's mean σ predicts where Cellpose fails in distribution; it does not (ρ = {{n_cp_sigma_rho}}), so we make no claim that the two are complementary there.
nucleus_text: At the level of single nuclei, σ is weak. The mean σ inside a predicted nucleus flags detections that match no reference nucleus with AUROC {{n_nuc_cs}} — slightly below a trivial 'dim nucleus' score on the same predictions ({{n_nuc_dim_cs}}) — and the U-Net's TTA disagreement does better on its own predictions ({{n_nuc_bt}}); the 3-seed ensemble does not help ({{n_nuc_ens}}). Discarding uncertain detections raises precision but lowers recall and F1 for every score (Figure 7). We therefore use per-nucleus σ only as a visual review aid and claim no advantage at this level.
prolif_text: Label-free counts reproduce the reference doubling time ({{n_pl_ref_dt}} h) with a mean absolute per-run bias of {{n_pl_cs_bias_all}} % (averaged over the three ChipStain seeds; {{n_pl_pm_bias_all}} % for the matched ImageNet U-Net, {{n_pl_bt_bias_all}} % for the scratch U-Net). The errors are driven by failing fields: in one ChipStain run {{n_pl_cs_collapsed}} fields collapse completely (no positive growth fit) and are therefore missing from the all-frames estimate — they count as failures, and that run's bias ({{n_pl_cs_worst_all}} %) understates its problem. The σ gate (threshold fixed on the validation split with a 5 % false-alarm budget; each frame's mean σ is taken relative to the median of the frames at the same time-point in the same run, so the gate needs a batch of frames per time-point) drops flagged frames and routes fields left with fewer than three frames to review. Compared on the same fields, most of the gain comes from that routing: ChipStain's mean bias is {{n_pl_cs_bias_all}} % on all fields, {{n_pl_cs_bias_same}} % on the fields the gate keeps without removing any frame, and {{n_pl_cs_bias_gate}} % gated (mean absolute per-field error {{n_pl_cs_mape_all}} → {{n_pl_cs_mape_same}} → {{n_pl_cs_mape_gate}} %). The gate helps the L1 models too (matched control {{n_pl_pm_bias_all}} → {{n_pl_pm_bias_same}} → {{n_pl_pm_bias_gate}} %; scratch {{n_pl_bt_bias_all}} → {{n_pl_bt_bias_same}} → {{n_pl_bt_bias_gate}} %), so it is not specific to ChipStain. It flags {{n_pl_cs_flagged}} of {{n_pl_frames_total}} ChipStain test frames ({{n_pl_cs_flag_pct}} %, far above the 5 % budget; the flags concentrate on a few fixed fields) and catches {{n_pl_cs_caught}} of the frames whose detection failed (F1 < 0.5): it catches catastrophic failures, not moderate ones. In total {{n_pl_cs_review}} field-runs are routed to review.
timelapse_text: On the full recording of one held-out field ({{n_tl_frames}} frames over 60 h, Figures 9–10) the label-free counts follow the real-stain counts with a mean error of {{n_tl_count_err}} % and give a doubling time of {{n_tl_dt_pred}} h versus {{n_tl_dt_real}} h, both counted with the same watershed — a growth curve from bright-field alone, without a single fluorescence exposure. Object-level agreement between the two segmentations is modest (median F1 {{n_tl_f1}}) because both use the simple watershed. Mean σ rises as the field becomes crowded and tracks per-frame failure (ρ(mean σ, 1 − F1) = {{n_tl_rho}}), which is confounded by density and time; frames after ≈37 h are beyond the densest training time-point. Five of the 240 frames are also test images; the other 235 were never used.
ablation_text: Table 3 changes one factor at a time (3 seeds each, no TTA). Robust effects — the CI excludes zero, at least two seeds are significant in that direction and none in the other — both improvements and degradations: {{n_abl_robust}}. Effects not listed are within run-to-run variation. Three conclusions follow. (i) The pixel-fidelity cost of ChipStain comes from the change of loss family: switching L1 to MSE robustly lowers SSIM and raises MAE, whereas adding the variance head (β-NLL vs MSE) has no robust effect. (ii) β trades fidelity against uncertainty: plain NLL (β = 0) ranks errors best but loses substantial fidelity (Pearson r {{n_b0_pearson}}, nuclei F1 {{n_b0_segf1}}); β = 1 keeps fidelity but loses ranking; β = 0.5 sits between. We fixed β = 0.5 before running the ablation, following the recommendation of the β-NLL authors [8]; the ablation shows it is a compromise, not the best choice on every axis. (iii) ImageNet pre-training robustly helps at the same learning rate, while lowering the learning rate alone hurts the scratch model.
neural_text: We applied the HeLa models to human iPSC-derived motor-neuron cultures (Christiansen et al. 2018, Condition A; 22 training and 3 test wells, bright-field z-stacks and widefield DAPI) — neurons in a dish, not an OoC. The rescale factor ({{n_neural_scale}}) and the bright-field z-plane ({{n_neural_z}}) were chosen on two validation wells with the ChipStain checkpoint and agree with a nucleus-size estimate computed from the DAPI images of all wells. Without weight updates (scale and plane chosen on the two labelled validation wells), ChipStain reaches Pearson r {{n_nz_cs_r}} with the real DAPI (U-Net {{n_nz_bu_r}}), but counting on the prediction is poor (F1 against the real-DAPI segmentation {{n_nz_cs_f1}}; count {{n_nz_cs_count}} %), and its mean σ ({{n_nz_cs_sigma}}) stays inside the HeLa test range ({{n_sigma_range}}): the uncertainty does not signal that the model is out of domain — consistent with §6.7. Fine-tuning from the HeLa weights with a single training well raises r to {{n_nf_cs_k1_r}} (F1 {{n_nf_cs_k1_f1}}), and with {{n_nf_kmax}} wells to {{n_nf_cs_k20_r}} (F1 {{n_nf_cs_k20_f1}}); starting from ImageNet instead gives {{n_nf_in_k1_r}} and {{n_nf_in_k20_r}}. These fine-tuning runs use one seed and the first k wells, so small differences are not meaningful; the experiment shows that a small paired set adapts the model to a new cell type and imaging system.
sec_limitations:
• No organ-on-a-chip data; one plate, one session. All validation uses 2-D cells in a well plate (HeLa) or a dish (neurons). The three HeLa wells come from one plate and one imaging session, so the hold-out measures well-to-well generalisation only. The shift test approximates some chip optics, not 3-D tissue, flow or PDMS autofluorescence. Before use on a chip, fine-tune on paired images from that device and re-check Tables 1, 5 and 7.
  • Fidelity cost. Against the matched ImageNet U-Net with TTA, ChipStain has equal correlation but {{n_pm_mae_rel}} % higher MAE and lower SSIM; the ablation traces this to the squared-error loss family.
  • Robustness and drift. Under blur and modality change every model's prediction fails and ChipStain's is not more robust (between the two L1 models under blur, worst with phase contrast). Whether σ then rises is seed-dependent for every model ({{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_ok}} ChipStain seeds), ChipStain's σ is the weakest of the three drift detectors on average, and any signal comes from the TTA term; σ is not a dependable drift alarm. A cheap input check (focus and encoder-feature distance) catches the simulated blur and modality shifts in every seed, but it was tested only on simulated shifts and flags {{n_qc_focus_gate_clean}} % of clean images from the new well.
  • Scope of the uncertainty. σ ranks pixel errors well and is near-calibrated in distribution, but at a single 20 % cut-off it is only slightly better than ranking by predicted intensity; at the nucleus level it is no better than a dim-nucleus heuristic; in distribution its frame-level signal is matched by the U-Net's TTA disagreement and largely reflects cell density; and the frame gate catches catastrophic, not moderate, failures.
  • Counting. A direct bright-field segmenter trained on matching labels counts nuclei better than counting on our prediction (§6.8).
  • Automatic references. F1 and counts are measured against StarDist labels on the real stain, not manual annotation; our watershed on the real stain reaches F1 {{n_real_segf1}} — a reference level, not a bound.
  • Training variability. One of three ChipStain seeds fails on two test fields (σ flags them); one U-Net seed loses {{n_bu_seed_gap}} nuclei F1. Retraining lands within the seed spread of Table 1, not on identical numbers; hence three seeds and seed-aware statistics throughout.
  • Target. mCherry-H2B is a genetically encoded reporter; on this dataset no dye is actually avoided. The value applies where such a reporter is unavailable.
  • Ethics. No human-subject, clinical or personal data. The main risk is over-trusting a hallucinated prediction, which σ and the gate are designed to reduce but cannot eliminate.
  • Proliferation gate. Most of the gated improvement comes from routing failing fields to review; the gate normalises each frame by the other frames at the same time-point, so it needs a batch of frames.
sec_impact:
Where ChipStain could help. Once fine-tuned on a small paired set from the target device, it could provide a quality-controlled, label-free nuclear channel for long recordings: growth and viability curves without fixation or repeated dye exposure, a freed fluorescence channel for a functional reporter, and a σ gate that keeps catastrophic frames out of the analysis (§6.10; the only proliferation evidence so far is from a well plate). Its mean σ should not be relied on as an imaging-drift alarm: under blur or a change of modality it rises only in some training runs (§6.7), so drift should be caught by the cheap input check of §6.7 (focus and encoder-feature distance), with its threshold re-set per device, and new imaging conditions confirmed with a few paired images. For pure nuclear counting a direct segmenter should be preferred (§6.8).

Neural OoC (the supporting organisation's focus). Neurons are post-mitotic, so label-free nuclear counts and nuclear condensation over weeks are a natural viability/neurotoxicity end-point; repeated live DNA dyes perturb such cultures, and reporter lines are rarely available for iPSC-derived neurons. §6.11 tests transfer to human iPSC-derived motor neurons.

Path to a chip. (1) Acquire a small set of paired bright-field / nuclear-stain images on the target device (we did not measure how many are needed on a chip; §6.11 measures it for neurons in a dish); (2) fine-tune from the released weights; (3) recalibrate σ with one scalar on held-out pairs; (4) set the frame gate on validation frames; (5) monitor mean σ in production as one signal among others, re-checking with paired images whenever the imaging changes. Inference runs on a CPU and depends on nothing proprietary. A trustworthy label-free nuclear channel is a prerequisite for the organisers' goal of AI-driven OoC digital twins: a twin fed unflagged hallucinations is worse than none.
shift_bullet: under blur or a phase-contrast input every model's prediction fails; ChipStain's is not more robust (r under 1 px blur {{n_shift_cs_r_def1}} vs {{n_shift_pre_r_def1}} matched / {{n_shift_bu_r_def1}} scratch; with phase contrast {{n_shift_cs_r_dpc}} vs {{n_shift_pre_r_dpc}} / {{n_shift_bu_r_dpc}}). Whether σ warns depends on the training run for every model (ChipStain: rises in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_ok}} seeds, falls in {{n_shift_cs_defocus_seeds_down}}), and averaged over seeds ChipStain's σ is the weakest shift detector of the three (blur AUROC {{n_shift_cs_sig_defocus}} vs {{n_shift_pre_sig_defocus}} / {{n_shift_bu_sig_defocus}}). Where a warning appears — as in the demo — it comes from the TTA disagreement, not the learned head. σ is therefore **not** a reliable drift alarm; added noise, by contrast, raises σ in every model and seed. **A cheap input check fills the gap** (no retraining): image focus (variance of the Laplacian) and the distance of the encoder features from the training set each flag {{n_qc_focus_gate_blur1}} % of 1 px-blurred and phase-contrast images in every seed; together with the σ gate, {{n_qc_fos_gate_noise10}} % of noisy images too. The price is {{n_qc_focus_gate_clean}} % false alarms on clean images of the new well, so the threshold should be re-set per plate or device.
nucleus_bullet: per-nucleus σ flags wrong detections only weakly (AUROC {{n_nuc_cs}}), no better than a dim-nucleus heuristic ({{n_nuc_dim_cs}}) and worse than the scratch U-Net's TTA disagreement on its own predictions ({{n_nuc_bt}}); we use it as a review aid, not a filter.
counting_bullet: counting on the prediction reaches nuclei F1 {{n_full_segf1}} (matched control {{n_pm_segf1}}); the dataset author's Cellpose model, which segments nuclei directly from bright-field, reaches {{n_cp_f1}}. For counting alone, direct segmentation is better; ChipStain adds a fluorescence-like image and a calibrated σ.
prolif_bullet: label-free counts give population doubling times with a mean bias of {{n_pl_cs_bias_all}} % (absolute per-run bias, mean over seeds; one run also has {{n_pl_cs_collapsed}} collapsed fields that count as failures). Gating frames by σ (threshold fixed on validation) lowers this to {{n_pl_cs_bias_gate}} % — mostly by routing failing fields to review: on the same fields without removing any frame the bias is already {{n_pl_cs_bias_same}} %. The gate helps the L1 baselines too (matched control {{n_pl_pm_bias_all}} → {{n_pl_pm_bias_same}} → {{n_pl_pm_bias_gate}} %: all fields → same fields → gated). On a 60 h, 240-frame recording: {{n_tl_dt_pred}} h vs {{n_tl_dt_real}} h from the real stain.
neural_bullet: on human iPSC-derived motor neurons (dish, not chip; one seed), the HeLa model applied without weight updates — the rescale factor and bright-field plane were chosen on 2 labelled validation wells — reaches Pearson r {{n_nz_cs_r}} but undercounts nuclei by about half, and its σ stays in the normal range (it does not warn). Fine-tuning on one well raises r to {{n_nf_cs_k1_r}} ({{n_nf_cs_k20_r}} with 20 wells), though nuclei counting stays weak (F1 {{n_nf_cs_k1_f1}}–{{n_nf_cs_k20_f1}}).
ablation_bullet: one factor at a time, 3 seeds each, robust effects in both directions: {{n_abl_robust}}. The fidelity cost comes from the L1 → squared-error loss change, not the variance head; β = 0.5 (fixed in advance, as recommended by the β-NLL authors) trades some error ranking for fidelity relative to β = 0.
limitations_short: Validation is on 2-D HeLa cells in one well plate (one imaging session) and neurons in a dish — **no chip data**. ChipStain costs {{n_pm_mae_rel}} % MAE against the matched control (from the squared-error loss). Its σ is strongest at ranking pixel errors, calibration and catching catastrophic frames in distribution; under blur or a new modality it is the weakest of the three drift detectors and warns only in some training runs (a cheap input check catches these simulated shifts instead, at {{n_qc_focus_gate_clean}} % false alarms on clean images), at the nucleus level it is no better than a simple heuristic, the proliferation gain comes mostly from routing failing fields to review, and a direct segmenter counts nuclei better. References are automatic StarDist labels. One of three seeds fails on two fields (σ flags them).
impact_short: Once fine-tuned on a few paired images from a device: a quality-controlled, label-free nuclear channel for long OoC recordings — growth and viability curves without dye exposure or fixation, a freed fluorescence channel, and a σ gate that keeps catastrophic frames out of the analysis (in distribution), with a cheap input check for drift. CPU inference, no proprietary dependencies.
neural_video: On human stem-cell-derived motor neurons, the model transfers partly even without retraining, and fine-tuning on a single well raises the correlation from {{n_nz_cs_r}} to {{n_nf_cs_k1_r}}.
calibration_bullet: ChipStain's σ is approximately calibrated without recalibration — the nominal 95 % interval covers {{n_cal_95}} % of test pixels (the validation-fitted scale would be ×{{n_cal_scale}}) — whereas the L1 U-Nets' TTA disagreement needs rescaling by ×{{n_cal_pm_scale}} (ImageNet) or ×{{n_cal_unet_scale}} (scratch): it can rank errors, not quantify them.
cellpose_pred_text: Replacing our watershed by Cellpose's generic fluorescence nuclei model, F1 on the real stain is {{n_cpp_real}} and on ChipStain's predictions {{n_cpp_pred}} — part of the gap is the segmenter, part is the prediction.
cellpose_shift_text: Under 2 px blur Cellpose's F1 drops from {{n_cps_clean}} to {{n_cps_blur2}} and it returns no uncertainty at all; ChipStain's σ does not reliably warn in that situation either (§6.7), so neither route protects a user against an imaging change.

inputqc_text: Because σ cannot be trusted to notice a shift, we tested two checks on the input that need no retraining, on the same 50 images, shifts and three seeds (scripts/input_qc.py). The focus check is model-free: the log variance of the Laplacian of the normalised bright-field image, scored as its distance from the training median (blur lowers it, noise raises it). The feature check is the Mahalanobis distance of the ChipStain encoder's deepest feature map (global average pool, 512 dimensions, Ledoit–Wolf covariance from the 200 training images). Each threshold is the 95th percentile of the score on the clean validation images, the same rule as the σ gate. Both checks separate blurred and phase-contrast images from clean ones almost perfectly (shift-detection AUROC: focus {{n_qc_focus_blur}} and {{n_qc_focus_dpc}}, features {{n_qc_feat_blur}} and {{n_qc_feat_dpc}}, against {{n_qc_sig_blur}} and {{n_qc_sig_dpc}} for total σ; Table 7c), and both flag {{n_qc_focus_gate_blur1}} % of images blurred by only 1 px and {{n_qc_focus_gate_dpc}} % of phase-contrast images in every seed (Table 7d). They also predict failure far better than σ (failure AUROC {{n_qc_focus_fail}} and {{n_qc_feat_fail}} vs {{n_qc_sig_fail}}), although with clean and shifted images pooled this mostly reflects that the shifted images are the ones that fail. The checks are complementary to σ: the focus check misses mild noise (it flags {{n_qc_focus_gate_noise10}} % of images with 10 % noise), which σ catches, and the feature check is seed-dependent on noise. Combining the focus check with the σ gate flags {{n_qc_fos_gate_blur1}} % of blurred, {{n_qc_fos_gate_noise10}} % of noisy (10 %; at least {{n_qc_fos_gate_noise10_min}} % in every seed) and {{n_qc_fos_gate_dpc}} % of phase-contrast images. The cost is false alarms. On clean test images the focus check flags {{n_qc_focus_gate_clean}} % (the combination {{n_qc_fos_gate_clean}} %), against 5 % expected on validation. These are fields of the held-out well whose focus differs slightly from the training wells, and their predictions are good (mean r {{n_qc_clean_r}}). They cost review time, not missed failures, and they show that the focus threshold should be re-set on a few clean images of each new plate or device. Recommended use: σ for trust inside the training domain, and a cheap input check for drift. These are simulated shifts; real chip optics remain untested.
